## Abstract

## Background

Preclinical evidence identifies the serotonin transporter (SERT, encoded by SLC6A4) as an immune checkpoint on CD8+ T cells, with selective serotonin reuptake inhib­ itors (SSRIs) enhancing antitumor immunity in synergy with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy. Whether this translates into clinical benefit for patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) is unknown. Using a target

trial emulation framework, we compared outcomes between SSRI users and benzo­ diazepine (BZD) users among patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving an ICI. Separately, in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which covers a different set of patients, we examined how SLC6A4 expression related to tumor immune-cell infiltration across cancers.

## Methods and findings

We emulated a target trial in the TriNetX federated electronic health record network (over 187 million patients), comparing SSRI with BZD treatment at first ICI administration under an intention-to-treat-analogue estimand. Eligible patients were adults with a solid tumor, a first ICI administration between 2015 and 2025, and a depressive or anxiety disorder recorded within the prior 365 days. Exposure required an active SSRI or BZD prescription overlapping the index date or starting within the preceding 90 days, not necessarily on that date. The

Estimates are hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Transcriptomic analyses used TCGA (8,272 tumor samples from 8,172 patients, 20 tumor types). Among 3,134 matched patients, SSRI use was associated with lower 2-year all-cause mortality (23.5% versus 34.4%; HR 0.627; 95% CI [0.549, 0.716]; p < 0.001; E-value 2.57). Composite immune-related adverse events (irAEs) were more frequent with SSRI use (HR 1.162; 95% CI [1.039, 1.299]; p = 0.008), driven by thyroid dysfunction (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), without increases in hepatitis, pneumonitis, or colitis (all p > 0.09). Newly coded distant metastases were less frequent in the SSRI group (HR 0.629; 95% CI [0.487, 0.811]; p < 0.001), and the 3 prespecified negative controls (nephrolithiasis, cholelithiasis, cataract) showed null associations (all p > 0.76). All 5 individually analyzable SSRIs were associated with lower mortality (HR range 0.61 to 0.71). In TCGA, SLC6A4 expression was inversely correlated with T-cell inflammation in 13 of 20 cancer types, and this organ-level pattern matched that of organ-specific irAEs. The main limitation is residual confounding: performance status, a clinician’s rating of everyday functional ability that strongly predicts cancer survival, is not recorded in the network, and BZDs are prescribed in different circumstances from SSRIs, so the groups may differ in ways matching cannot capture. The TCGA analyses used bulk tumor tissue from patients not treated with ICIs, so they cannot localize SLC6A4 to particular cells or show that SSRIs alter the tumor microenvironment.

## Conclusions

In this study, SSRI use was associated with lower mortality and organ-selective immune activation compared with BZD use among ICI-treated patients with psychiatric comorbidity. Transcriptomic evidence supports biological plausibility. These findings warrant prospective evaluation of SSRI repurposing as an ICI adjuvant.

## What did the researchers do and find?

• Using electronic health records from a large international network, we compared

1,567 people taking an SSRI with 1,567 people taking a benzodiazepine, all of whom had a solid tumor and depression or anxiety and were beginning immuno­ therapy, matched on 49 clinical characteristics.

• Over 2 years, 23.5% of the SSRI group died compared with 34.4% of the benzo­

diazepine group, and the SSRI group also had fewer newly recorded secondary tumors and fewer referrals to hospital and to palliative care.

• The SSRI group had more immune-related side effects overall, almost entirely

thyroid problems, with no increase in inflammation of the liver, lungs, or bowel, and in tumor tissue from more than 8,000 cancers in a separate group of patients, higher activity of the serotonin transporter gene went with fewer immune cells inside the tumor.

## What do these findings mean?

• SSRIs, which are already widely prescribed to people with cancer, were

associated with better outcomes during immunotherapy, and both the pattern of side effects and the tumor gene activity data are consistent with an effect on the immune system; a randomized trial is needed to test this directly.

• Because people were not randomly assigned to receive one medicine or the

other, these results show an association and cannot show that SSRIs caused the better outcomes.

• The records do not capture how well or unwell a person was when treatment

started, and benzodiazepines are often given at times of acute distress or wors­ ening illness, so part of the difference may reflect how ill people were rather than the medicine itself.

## Introduction

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed treatment across multiple solid tumor types, yet only a fraction of patients achieve durable responses [1]. Depression and anxiety affect 20–40% of patients with cancer who receive immunotherapy [2] and are associated with worse treatment outcomes and survival [3]; both depression and serotonergic signaling are increasingly recognized to interact with immune function [4,5], underscoring the clinical importance of psychotropic medication choices in this population.

A landmark preclinical study by Li and colleagues [6] identified the serotonin transporter (SERT, encoded by SLC6A4) as an immune checkpoint on CD8+ T cells. SERT-mediated serotonin reuptake suppressed T-cell receptor signaling through the 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor (5-HTR) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, while pharma­ cologic SERT inhibition with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) restored intratumoral serotonin and enhanced antitumor immunity. In murine models, SSRI combined with anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (anti-PD-1) therapy produced synergistic tumor regression, establishing a direct mechanistic link between serotonergic signaling and check­ point blockade efficacy. These findings were independently supported by studies demonstrating enhanced immunosurveil­ lance through serotonergic mechanisms, including peripheral serotonin attenuation [7], pleiotropic SSRI-mediated immune enhancement [8], and tumor-associated macrophage modulation [9].

Because SLC6A4 encodes the molecular target of SSRIs and the principal route by which serotonin is cleared from the tumor microenvironment, it is the logical node linking serotonergic signaling to checkpoint immunity, and, among the genes of the serotonin pathway, the one most likely to be modulated by routine clinical SSRI exposure.

Clinical evidence for this SSRI-ICI interaction remains limited. Magagnoli and colleagues [10] reported a suggestive survival benefit with fluoxetine among Veterans Affairs patients receiving PD-1/programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1) ther­ apy, but the analysis included only 34 exposed patients. Observational studies have linked emotional distress to worse ICI outcomes and reduced immune-related adverse event (irAE) incidence [11,12], but none have directly compared seroto­ nergic versus nonserotonergic psychotropic agents in a design that reduces confounding by indication through an active comparator. Large-scale clinical evidence with active-comparator controls and translational validation is therefore lacking, leaving the question unresolved between preclinical discovery and clinical application.

Because no randomized trial has compared serotonergic with nonserotonergic psychotropic agents in this setting, we used target trial emulation [13], an approach that applies the design principles of a randomized trial, namely explicit eligibility, defined treatment strategies, a common time zero, and a prespecified estimand, to observational data, reducing biases such as immortal-time and prevalent-user bias and making the intended comparison explicit when a randomized trial is unavailable. Because treatment was not randomly assigned, the resulting estimates remain associations rather than randomized comparisons.

Here, we report a target trial emulation comparing SSRI versus benzodiazepine (BZD) use among 3,134 propensity score-matched patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving ICIs, drawn from the TriNetX federated electronic health record network. The active-comparator design isolates the serotonergic mechanism by con­ trasting SERT inhibition (SSRI) against gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) signaling (BZD) in patients with equivalent psychiatric comorbidity. Twenty prespecified outcomes organized across 4 mechanistic pathways (immune enhancement, disease trajectory, BZD-specific harm, and negative controls) are used to discriminate among competing mechanistic explanations. To investigate the biological basis of these clinical findings, we examine SLC6A4 expression and immune microenvironment features across 20 solid tumor types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), including an organ-level cross-validation linking tissue-specific SLC6A4-immune associations to clinical irAE patterns. We asked whether the choice of psychotropic agent at ICI initiation is associated with subsequent outcomes, and hypothesized that, among patients with depression or anxiety who initiate an ICI, initiation of an SSRI rather than a benzodiazepine is associated with lower 2-year all-cause mortality, and that any such association is accompanied by an organ-selective increase in immune-related adverse events in the tissues where SLC6A4 expression tracks most closely with reduced immune-cell infiltration.

## Methods

Study design and data source

This retrospective cohort study used an active-comparator, new-user design [14] within the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, a federated electronic health record (EHR) platform integrating de-identified data from over 187 million patients

across 172 healthcare organizations. We compared outcomes between SSRI and benzodiazepine (BZD) users among patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who received immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy between January 2015 and December 2025. The active-comparator design reduces confounding by indication [15], as both groups carry psychiatric diagnoses and receive psychotropic treatment, while providing a mechanistic contrast between sero­ tonergic (SERT inhibition) and GABAergic (GABA-A agonism) pathways. This study is reported in accordance with the STROBE reporting guideline [16] (S1 Checklist) and the TARGET guideline for emulating a target trial [17] (S2 Checklist). The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Tri-Service General Hospital, National Defense Medical Center (TSGHIRB No. E202516013), with a certificate of review exemption.

The hypothetical target trial and its emulation are specified in full in the pre-specified analysis plan (S1 Protocol): eligi­ ble adults with a solid tumor and a documented depressive or anxiety disorder would be randomly assigned, at the time of first ICI administration (time zero), to initiate an SSRI or a benzodiazepine and followed for overall survival and prespec­ ified secondary outcomes under an intention-to-treat estimand. In the emulation, randomization is replaced by 1:1 pro­ pensity score matching on 49 baseline covariates, time zero is the first ICI administration, and follow-up, outcomes, and the causal contrast are operationalized from the electronic health record. Variables that a trial would balance but that are unmeasured here, notably Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite-instability status, are addressed through negative-control outcomes, E-values, and the sensitivity analyses described below. The target trial and its emulation are also specified component by component in S1 Protocol (Section 3) and shown schematically in Fig 1.

Study population

Patients were eligible if they met all of the following criteria: (1) age 18 years or older at the index date; (2) a solid malignant neoplasm (International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision, Clinical Modification [ICD-10-CM] C00-C80) documented on or before the index date; (3) a first administration of any of the 13 US Food and Drug Administration-approved immune checkpoint inhibitors listed in S8 Table (including pembrolizumab, nivolumab, atezolizumab, durvalumab, and ipilimumab) between January 1, 2015 and December 31, 2025, which defined the index date (time zero); (4) major depressive disorder (F32, F33), generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1), or anxiety disorder not otherwise specified (F41.9) recorded within 365 days before the index date; (5) an active prescription for an SSRI or a benzodiazepine within 90 days before to 14 days after the index date; (6) at least 365 days of electronic health record data before the index date; and (7) at least 1 day of follow-up after the index date. The SSRI group comprised users of sertraline, escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, citalopram, or fluvoxamine without concurrent benzodiazepine use, and the comparator group comprised users of lorazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, diazepam, temazepam, oxazepam, or chlordiazepoxide without concurrent antidepressant use (S8 and S9 Tables). Exposure was therefore ascertained from an active prescription in the window from 90 days before to 14 days after the index date: patients were new users of ICI therapy, and their psychotropic treatment could already have been in place before the first ICI infusion rather than starting on that day.

Patients were excluded if they had any of the following: (1) hematologic malignancy (C81-C96) at any time before the index date; (2) pre-existing autoimmune disease requiring immunosuppressive therapy; (3) HIV infection (B20) at any time; (4) a history of solid organ or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (Z94); (5) a schizophrenia spectrum disorder (F20-F29) or bipolar disorder (F30-F31) at any time; (6) systemic corticosteroid therapy at 10 mg or more of prednisone equivalent per day for 14 days or longer within the 30 days before the index date; (7) delirium (F05) within 30 days before the index date; (8) palliative care (Z51.5) within 30 days before the index date; (9) concurrent prescriptions for both an SSRI and a benzodiazepine overlapping the index date; or (10) a prescription for any non-SSRI antidepressant (serotoninnorepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, tricyclic antidepressant, or monoamine oxidase inhibitor) overlapping the index date. Mutual exclusivity of SSRI and benzodiazepine use was assessed at baseline, within the exposure window of 90 days

Outcomes

The primary outcome was overall survival (time from first ICI to death; 2-year window). Follow-up began on day 30 after ICI initiation, a prespecified 30-day landmark that aligns the survival window with the new-diagnosis outcome window and reduces immortal-time and early-death bias [19], and continued until death, last EHR contact, or day 730, whichever came first. The 2-year window was prespecified as the clinically relevant horizon for first-line ICI benefit and to harmonize follow-up across organizations with differing data maturity; a sensitivity analysis without time-window restriction was also performed. Twenty secondary outcomes were organized across 4 prespecified mechanistic pathways, which label the hypothesized mechanisms the study was designed to discriminate among and are not claims of established causation: path A (SSRI immune enhancement), path B (better disease trajectory), path C (BZD-specific harm), and path D (negative controls). Path A comprised 6 outcomes: thyroid dysfunction (new thyroid immune-related adverse event; E03, E06), a composite of new immune-related adverse events across 10 organ systems, a new systemic corticosteroid prescription, newly coded distant metastasis (C77, C78, C79), time to next treatment, and the number of ICI administrations during follow-up. Path B comprised 6 outcomes: an emergency department visit, unplanned hospitalization, palliative or hos­ pice referral (Z51.5), a new psychiatric diagnosis (F32, F33, F41, F43), opioid dose escalation, and suicidal ideation or self-harm (R45.851, T14.91, X71-X83). Path C comprised 5 outcomes: falls (W00-W19, R29.6), fractures (traumatic or osteoporotic fragility), delirium (F05, R41.0, R41.82), sepsis or severe infection (A41, R65.2, A49), and venous thrombo­ embolism (I26, I82). Path D comprised 3 outcomes without biological plausibility for differential SSRI-BZD association, serving as bias indicators: nephrolithiasis (N20), cholelithiasis (K80), and cataract (H25, H26). Unless otherwise specified, outcomes were ascertained between days 30 and 730 after ICI initiation; the per-outcome ascertainment rules and the complete code lists are given in S10 and S11 Tables.

As a progression-sensitive proxy, because radiographic progression-free survival cannot be ascertained in this net­ work, we defined time to next treatment as the time from ICI initiation to the start of a new systemic anticancer agent that was not part of the baseline regimen (chemotherapy, a protein kinase inhibitor, or a non-ICI therapeutic monoclonal antibody or antibody-drug conjugate), with continued or re-initiated ICI not counted as an event and death censored. To assess whether differential surveillance could account for differences in newly coded metastases, we also compared the per-patient frequency of cross-sectional imaging (computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography-computed tomography, and bone scintigraphy) between groups during follow-up.

Statistical analysis

Time-to-event outcomes were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier estimation with log-rank tests and Cox proportional hazards regression. The single primary outcome (overall survival) was prespecified; secondary-outcome p values are descriptive and unadjusted for multiplicity, and secondary findings are interpreted as hypothesis-generating. The proportional hazards assumption was tested using Schoenfeld residuals, and restricted mean survival time (RMST) is reported for the primary outcome. Palliative or hospice referral (p = 0.032) and venous thromboembolism (p = 0.042) violated it, so their hazard ratios are period-averaged effects. E-values were calculated following VanderWeele and Ding [20] to quantify the mini­ mum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would need with both exposure and outcome to explain away the observed result (S6 Table). Three prespecified sensitivity analyses were performed: per-protocol (N = 695 matched pairs), US-only (N = 1,450 pairs), and dual SSRI plus BZD versus BZD-only (N = 2,457 pairs).

The primary analysis estimates the intention-to-treat-analogue effect of SSRI versus benzodiazepine treatment at ICI initiation, consistent with the pre-specified analysis plan; the per-protocol analysis is a sensitivity analysis. We prioritized the intention-to-treat analogue because it matches the pre-specified estimand and does not require censoring at treatment switching, which on this federated platform cannot be corrected by inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting because patient-level data cannot be exported. These 7 analyses are listed as post hoc in S1 Protocol (Section 11) and are interpreted as hypothesis-generating and supportive rather than confirmatory. TCGA pan-cancer transcriptomic analyses

To assess whether the serotonin transporter gene SLC6A4 associates with the extent of immune-cell infiltration across human cancers, we analyzed RNA-seq data from 8,272 tumor samples contributed by 8,172 patients across 20 solid tumor types in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA); 100 patients contributed more than one tumor sample, and no patient appeared in more than one tumor type. Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) [21] was used to compute immune function scores (T-cell Inflamed Gene Expression Profile [GEP] [22], Cytotoxic Score [23]) and classify tumors into 3 immune phenotypes (Inflamed, Excluded, and Desert) [24]. Spearman correlations between SLC6A4 expression and immune scores were computed per cancer type with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Organ-level concordance was assessed by mapping tissue-specific SLC6A4-immune correlations to clinical organ-specific irAE hazard ratios for 5 organ systems with direct anatomical correspondence. A random-effects meta-analysis (restricted maximum likelihood estimator, Hartung–Knapp confidence interval) of SLC6A4 expression and overall survival was per­ formed across 18 evaluable cancer types. Full details are provided in the S1 Text and S13, S14 Tables.

To test whether the focus on SLC6A4 was justified rather than arbitrary, we extended the transcriptomic analysis to the entire serotonin pathway, computing the correlation of each of 20 pathway genes (the transporter SLC6A4, 14 serotonin receptors, the synthesis enzymes TPH1, TPH2, and DDC, and the degradation enzymes MAOA and MAOB) with three orthogonal immune signatures across the 20 tumor types, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The TCGA analyses are cross-sectional and use bulk tumor tissue from patients not treated with ICIs, so they cannot localize SLC6A4 to particular cells or show that SSRIs alter the tumor microenvironment.

## Results

Study cohort and primary outcome

From 187,237,420 patients in the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network, 11,337 met eligibility criteria (Fig 2). After exclud­ ing 4,176 dual SSRI plus BZD users, propensity score matching yielded 1,567 pairs (Table 1). All covariates were well balanced (all SMD < 0.10; complete covariate balance in S20 Table). Median follow-up was 395 days (SSRI) and 349 days (BZD).

SSRI use was associated with significantly lower 2-year all-cause mortality compared with BZD use (368 of 1,567 [23.5%] versus 539 of 1,567 [34.4%]; hazard ratio [HR] 0.627; 95% confidence interval [CI] [0.549, 0.716]; p < 0.001; Fig 3). The proportional hazards assumption was met (Schoenfeld p = 0.825). The Kaplan–Meier estimated absolute risk difference increased from 3.0% at 3 months to 14.9% at 24 months. RMST analysis showed a 2.1-month difference in restricted mean survival time (SSRI, 19.1 months versus BZD, 17.0 months; S2 Fig). The E-value for the primary outcome was 2.57 (95% CI bound, 2.14).

Mechanistic pathway outcomes and organ-selective irAE

Twenty secondary outcomes were assessed across 4 pathways (Fig 4 and S5 Table; key outcomes summarized in Table 2).

In path A (immune enhancement), composite irAE incidence was significantly higher with SSRIs (771 of 1,567 [49.2%] versus 682 of 1,567 [43.5%]; HR 1.162; 95% CI [1.039, 1.299]; p = 0.008). Thyroid dysfunction was the primary driver (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), while hepatitis (HR 0.711; 95% CI [0.474, 1.065]; p = 0.096), pneumonitis (HR 1.023; 95% CI [0.734, 1.427]; p = 0.892), and colitis (HR 1.130; 95% CI [0.913, 1.397]; p = 0.260) did not differ significantly (S4 Table). New distant metastases were significantly less frequent with SSRI use among patients without baseline metastases (102 of 595 [17.1%] versus 142 of 569 [25.0%]; HR 0.629; 95% CI [0.487, 0.811]; p < 0.001). Time to next treatment, a progression proxy, was also longer with SSRI use (HR 0.876; 95% CI [0.811, 0.946]; p = 0.001; Tables 2 and S5).

In path B (better disease trajectory), SSRI users had lower rates of emergency department visits (HR 0.783; 95% CI [0.689, 0.891]; p < 0.001), hospitalization (HR 0.730; 95% CI [0.651, 0.817]; p < 0.001), palliative or hospice referral (HR 0.563; 95% CI [0.474, 0.668]; p < 0.001), and opioid escalation (HR 0.779; 95% CI [0.713, 0.851]; p < 0.001). New psychi­ atric diagnoses did not differ (HR 1.024; 95% CI [0.933, 1.124]; p = 0.610).

In path C (BZD-specific harm), delirium (HR 0.696; 95% CI [0.547, 0.886]; p = 0.003) and sepsis (HR 0.699; 95% CI [0.564, 0.866]; p = 0.001) were significantly lower with SSRIs. Falls (HR 1.014; 95% CI [0.797, 1.290]; p = 0.913) and frac­ tures (HR 1.028; 95% CI [0.830, 1.272]; p = 0.803) did not differ.

In path D (negative controls), all 3 outcomes showed null associations: nephrolithiasis (HR 1.042; 95% CI [0.767, 1.414]; p = 0.793), cholelithiasis (HR 1.043; 95% CI [0.764, 1.424]; p = 0.792), and cataract (HR 1.047; 95% CI [0.778, 1.410]; p = 0.761).

Organ-level cross-validation

Mapping clinical irAE HRs to TCGA SLC6A4-immune correlations across 5 organs revealed concordance between reduced tumor immune-cell infiltration in the transcriptomic data and clinical immune activation (Fig 5D; S14 Table). ## Discussion

In this target trial emulation of 3,134 patients with a solid tumor and depression or anxiety who were receiving ICIs, SSRI use was associated with a 37% lower hazard of death over 2 years compared with BZD use (HR 0.627; 95% CI [0.549, 0.716]). This mortality association was accompanied by increased immune-related adverse events, reduced metastatic progression, and a favorable disease trajectory including lower rates of hospitalization and palliative referral. Three null negative control outcomes, consistent results across per-protocol and US-only sensitivity analyses, and an E-value of 2.57 support the robustness of these findings.

The prespecified mechanistic pathway framework helps distinguish among competing mechanisms. Path A (immune enhancement) showed the most mechanistically informative pattern: composite irAE was significantly increased, driven selectively by thyroid dysfunction (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]) without significant increases in hepatitis, pneumonitis, or colitis. This organ selectivity suggests serotonergic modulation of T-cell activity concentrated in the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis [25,26] rather than generalized immune activation, and the absence of high-severity irAE increase provides a favorable safety signal. Reduced coded new metastases among patients without baseline metastases are consistent with, but does not by itself establish, an antitumor immune effect; comparable imagingsurveillance frequency between groups argues against differential detection; death is, however, a competing event for metastasis coding, and because we did not perform a formal competing-risk analysis this association is cause-specific rather than a subdistribution estimate. Path B (disease trajectory) showed consistently favorable results including significantly reduced hospitalization, palliative referral, and opioid escalation, reflecting both potential tumor control

All 5 individual SSRIs were associated with significantly lower mortality, supporting a class-wide SERT inhibition mechanism rather than agentspecific off-target effects.

The TCGA analysis addresses whether the inverse association between SLC6A4 expression and tumor immunecell infiltration is tissue-specific, a question with direct clinical relevance for predicting organ-selective irAE. Across 20 solid tumor types, SLC6A4 expression was inversely correlated with T-cell inflammation in the majority of cancers and associated with the Immune Desert phenotype, a pan-cancer pattern rather than a single-tumor observation. Critically, organ-level cross-validation showed that the thyroid, where the inverse SLC6A4-immune association was strongest, was also the organ with a significant clinical irAE increase (HR 1.199; 95% CI [1.053, 1.366]; p = 0.006), while tissues with no SLC6A4-immune association (liver, lung) showed no irAE increase. Colon showed a comparable transcriptomic correla­ tion (rho −0.326; FDR < 0.001) without a significant clinical increase (HR 1.130; 95% CI [0.913, 1.397]; p = 0.260). SLC6A4 was not independently prognostic in the pre-immunotherapy TCGA cohort, reinforcing that this axis becomes clinically relevant only in the context of checkpoint blockade.

These transcriptomic findings are best read as an independent, mechanism-oriented line of evidence rather than a demonstration that SSRIs cause the clinical associations: the TCGA samples are not from patients treated with SSRIs, so they support biological plausibility, not causation. Whether SSRI exposure actually shifts an immune-desert tumor toward an inflamed phenotype cannot be answered with cross-sectional data and would require a prospective cohort treated with ICIs with or without an SSRI, with paired pre- and post-treatment sampling and peripheral immune biomarkers, to estab­ lish such a conversion directly.

This study has several limitations. First, unmeasured confounders may introduce residual bias despite 49 propensity score-matched covariates. ECOG performance status, the most concerning potential confounder, is not captured in the TriNetX database; if SSRI users had systematically better functional status, this could partly explain the survival difference. PD-L1 expression, tumor mutational burden, and microsatellite instability status were similarly unavailable. Established pharmacologic modifiers of ICI efficacy, notably baseline systemic corticosteroids [28] and antibiotic exposure [29], were addressed by excluding baseline systemic corticosteroid users and matching on baseline medication classes, although residual effects cannot be excluded. However, the E-value of 2.57 indicates that an unmeasured confounder would need a strong association with both exposure and outcome to fully explain the result, and the 3 null negative control outcomes [30] argue against systematic residual confounding. Second, ICD-10-based irAE identification lacks specificity for immune-mediated etiology [31–33]; thyroid events may include non-ICI-related hypothyroidism, and neuropathy codes capture both immune-mediated and chemotherapy-induced neuropathy. Nonetheless, this misclassification would bias irAE results toward the null, making the observed thyroid signal conservative. Third, the two drug classes are prescribed in different clinical circumstances: benzodiazepines are frequently given as needed for acute anxiety, insomnia, or distress around disease progression, so the comparator group may carry a worse underlying trajectory, a form of confounding by indication that would favor SSRIs. Several findings argue against this fully explaining the result, including preservation of the association across the prespecified sensitivity analyses, an E-value of 2.57, and an association that persisted against a comparator receiving neither agent (HR 0.753; 95% CI [0.605, 0.939]); the per-protocol estimate was directionally stronger (HR 0.575; 95% CI [0.472, 0.702]) but, being susceptible to informative censoring that cannot be corrected on this federated platform, is treated only as a sensitivity analysis; residual differences in psychiatric severity or care intensity nonetheless cannot be excluded, and the neither-agent comparison may itself be biased if untreated patients have milder illness or lower healthcare engagement. Fourth, SSRI prescription may proxy for integrated psycho-oncology care or more comprehensive healthcare engagement rather than a direct pharmacologic effect; however, the consistent association across all 5 individual SSRIs and the organ-selective irAE pattern are difficult to explain by differential care engagement

In conclusion, SSRI use was associated with lower mortality, organ-selective immune activation, and a more favorable disease trajectory compared with BZD use among patients with psychiatric comorbidity who were receiving ICIs. Tran­ scriptomic evidence that SLC6A4 expression is inversely associated with tumor immune-cell infiltration across human can­ cers provides biological plausibility. These findings support prospective evaluation of SSRI repurposing as an ICI adjuvant in a randomized trial, with immune-related adverse events and peripheral immune biomarkers as co-primary end points to confirm the proposed mechanism.
